1.1: The very first verse of the Rigveda! The poet says, 'I praise Agni.' Agni is the sacred fire, called the 'purohita' — the one placed in front — because in every worship the fire stands at the centre. He is also called the best giver of treasures.
1.2: Agni was praised by the rishis of long ago, and he is praised by people today too. The poet says Agni will bring the gods here — like a host who invites guests to a feast.
1.3: Through Agni, people receive good things that grow day by day: food, family and a good name. Think of how a kitchen fire feeds a whole household every single day.
1.4: When people make an offering, Agni surrounds it with his flames and carries it to the gods. That is why fire is called the messenger between the earth and the sky.
1.5: Agni is wise, truthful and full of glory. The poet invites him: 'Come, O god, and bring the other gods with you!'
1.6: Whatever good Agni promises to someone who worships him, he keeps that promise. The poet calls him 'Aṅgiras', an old name, and says: your truth is that you always give.
1.7: Every day, in the morning and the evening, we come to Agni with our prayers and bow to him. Agni is called the one who chases away the darkness — just like a lamp at night.
1.8: Agni rules over the worship, guards Ṛta (the true order of the world) and shines brightly. He grows bigger in his own home — the fire-altar — when people feed him wood and ghee.
1.9: A loving ending: 'Be easy to reach for us, Agni, like a father is for his son. Stay with us for our good.' The poet wants the divine to feel as close as a parent.

32.1: The poet begins, 'Now I will tell the brave deeds of Indra!' Indra, holding the thunderbolt (vajra), killed the serpent Vṛtra, set the waters free and opened channels in the mountains for rivers to flow.
32.2: Vṛtra was lying on the mountain. The divine craftsman Tvaṣṭṛ had made Indra's thunderbolt. When the serpent was struck, the waters rushed down to the sea like mooing cows running home.
32.3: Indra drank Soma from three special cups to become strong like a bull. Then Maghavan ('the generous one' — another name for Indra) picked up the thunderbolt and struck the first-born of the serpents.
32.4: When the serpent fell, its tricks stopped working. Indra then brought out the Sun, the Dawn and the Sky — light returned to the world. No enemy was left to stand against him.
32.5: With his great thunderbolt, Indra broke Vṛtra apart. The giant serpent fell to the ground like a tree trunk cut down by an axe.
32.6: Vṛtra was proud and foolish and challenged the mighty Indra. But he could not stand the clash of weapons and fell, crushing his own strongholds as he went down.
32.7: Even without hands and feet, Vṛtra kept challenging Indra, who struck him between the shoulders. He had pretended to be strong, but now he lay broken. Being boastful does not make you strong!
32.8: Now the waters flow happily over the fallen Vṛtra, like a river bursting its banks. The waters he once held prisoner now run freely above him.
32.9: Vṛtra's mother, Dānu, tried to protect her son, but Indra struck her too. She fell beside him like a cow lying next to her calf.
32.10: Vṛtra's body is carried away by the never-stopping rivers and sinks into darkness. The blocker is gone; the flow of life continues.
32.11: The waters had been kept like cows locked up by a thief, guarded by the serpent. When Indra struck Vṛtra, he opened the cave and let the waters out.
32.12: Indra brushed off the attack as easily as a horse flicks its tail. He won back the cows and the Soma, and set the Seven Rivers flowing. 'Seven Rivers' means the rivers of the Rigveda's homeland, Sapta Sindhu.
32.13: Vṛtra tried lightning, thunder, hail and mist — nothing helped him. When the two fought, Indra won the victory forever.
32.14: A surprising verse: after winning, Indra felt fear for a moment and fled across ninety-nine rivers like a frightened hawk. Even heroes can feel afraid — courage means acting even with fear.
32.15: Indra is king of everything that moves and everything that stays still, of tame and wild animals. He holds everything together, like the rim of a wheel holds all its spokes.

50.1: The Sun's rays lift him high into the sky so that everyone in the whole world can see. Sūrya, the Sun god, knows everything that lives because he looks at it all.
50.2: When the Sun rises, the stars slip away like thieves at the end of the night. The poet makes it sound like a funny little chase across the sky!
50.3: The Sun's rays are seen far away, shining over all the lands, bright like blazing flames. They are like messengers announcing that a new day has come.
50.4: 'You are quick and beautiful, O Sun, the maker of light! You light up the whole shining sky.'
50.5: The Sun goes to the gods and also comes to people — his light is for everyone, so all can see.
50.6: Varuṇa, the guardian of truth, watches the busy world of people through the Sun's bright eye. The poet imagines the Sun as the eye of the sky.
50.7: The Sun travels across the sky and the air, measuring out our days with his beams. Every day is marked by sunrise and sunset.
50.8: Seven bay (reddish-brown) horses pull the Sun's chariot, and the Sun has hair made of rays. Many people link the seven horses with the seven colours of the rainbow.
50.9: The Sun has yoked his seven bright mares, called 'the daughters of the chariot', and drives out in the morning with his own team.
50.10: Looking at the light rising above the darkness, we come to the Sun, the highest light among the gods. This is a favourite morning prayer for many people.
50.11: Now a healing prayer: 'O Sun, rising today, take away my heart's sickness and my yellow colour.' People long ago noticed that sunlight helps the body feel better.
50.12: A playful verse: 'Let us give my yellowness to the green parrots and the starling birds, and to the yellow haritāla trees!' The poet sends the illness away to things that are yellow anyway.
50.13: The Sun, son of Aditi, has risen with all his power. The poet asks to be kept safe from anyone who wishes him harm.

89.1: 'Let good and noble thoughts come to us from every side!' The poet asks that blessings come from everywhere, never stopped, so the gods are always with us and look after us every day.
89.2: The poet asks for the kindness and gifts of the gods, and their friendship. He also asks them to give us a long life.
89.3: We call many gods with an old hymn: Bhaga (good luck), Mitra (friendship), Aditi (mother of gods), Varuṇa, Soma, the twin Aśvins and Sarasvatī. Each brings a different blessing.
89.4: May the Wind, Mother Earth and Father Sky bring us healing medicine. Even the stones that press the Soma are asked to help! The whole of nature is invited to make us well.
89.5: We call on the Lord of all things moving and still, who inspires our minds. May Pūṣan, the god who guards travellers and paths, keep us safe and help us grow.
89.6: This verse is a well-known peace prayer: may Indra, Pūṣan, Tārkṣya (a swift divine bird-horse) and Bṛhaspati (lord of prayer) all bless us with well-being.
89.7: The Maruts, the storm gods riding spotted deer, are called too. All the gods are invited to come and protect us.
89.8: The most famous verse: 'O gods, may we hear good things with our ears and see good things with our eyes.' With strong bodies, we want to live the full life the gods give us. Many schools say this prayer every day.
89.9: People hoped to live a hundred autumns — a hundred years — long enough to see their children become parents. The poet asks the gods not to cut life short in the middle.
89.10: A beautiful ending: Aditi is the sky, the air, mother, father and child, all the gods, all people — everything that was born and will be born. It shows the idea that everything is connected in one.

113.1: 'The best of all lights has come!' Dawn is born, bright and spreading far. Night has stepped aside so that the Sun can rise, making room for the Morning.
113.2: Bright Dawn arrives with her shining 'children' — the rays of light. Dark Night gives her home to her. The two are sisters who never die; they follow each other and keep changing the colour of the sky.
113.3: Night and Dawn share one never-ending road through the sky, taking turns as the gods taught them. They look different, but they agree and never fight or bump into each other. A lovely lesson about sharing!
113.4: Dawn leads all the happy morning sounds — birds singing, cows mooing. She opens the doors of the sky, shows us the world's treasures and wakes up every living creature.
113.5: Dawn wakes the sleeper curled up in bed: one to enjoy, one to earn, one to pray, and gives those who could see only a little a wider view. Morning gives everyone a fresh chance.
113.6: Dawn sends each person to their own work: one to lead, one to earn fame, one to earn a living, one to labour. Every job matters, and the morning calls everyone to do theirs.
113.7: We see her: the Daughter of the Sky, a young girl glowing in shining clothes. 'O queen of all earthly treasures, shine on us kindly this morning!'
113.8: Each Dawn is the first of all the mornings still to come, and she follows all the mornings that came before. She wakes up the living, but she cannot wake those who have died.
113.9: Dawn makes people light the morning fire (Agni), shows the world through the Sun's eye and wakes people to pray. By doing this, she serves the gods well.
113.10: The poet wonders: how long until all the dawns — past and future — are together? Dawn seems to long for the dawns before her and shines happily along with the ones to come.
113.11: A deep thought: the people who watched the dawns long ago are gone. Now we, the living, see her light, and one day others will see it after us. So make good use of today!
113.12: Dawn is born from Ṛta, the true order of the world, and she protects it. She brings joy, wakes pleasant voices and brings food for the gods. 'Shine on us, Dawn, this morning!'
113.13: Dawn has shone since the beginning of time and shines today too, full of riches. She will shine on all the days to come — she never grows old.
113.14: At the edges of the sky Dawn shines and throws off the blanket of darkness. She comes on her chariot pulled by reddish horses, waking up the world.
113.15: Dawn brings all the blessings that keep us alive. She is the last of the countless mornings that are gone and the first of all the bright mornings yet to come.
113.16: 'Get up! Breath and life have come back to us!' Darkness has gone and light is coming. Dawn has made a path for the Sun. Every morning feels like starting life again.
113.17: The poet rises in the morning, weaving his song like a cloth to praise the shining Dawns. He asks Dawn to give long life and children to the one who praises her.
113.18: The poet hopes that the dawns will bring strong children, cows and horses to the person who offers worship, and that his songs will be louder than the wind.
113.19: Dawn is called the mother of the gods and the shining glory of Aditi, the sign that worship has begun. The poet asks her to bless his prayers and help his people do well.
113.20: A closing prayer: may Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, the river Sindhu, Earth and Sky also give us the good things that the Dawns bring.

164.1: THE RIDDLE HYMN by the seer Dīrghatamas. It is full of puzzles, and even scholars disagree about many answers. Here three 'brothers' are often explained as three forms of fire: the Sun in the sky, lightning in the middle air and the sacred fire on earth, sprinkled with ghee.
164.2: Riddle: seven yoke a one-wheeled chariot pulled by one horse with seven names. The wheel has three hubs and never wears out, and all worlds rest on it. A common answer: the Sun's chariot — the wheel is the year, and the three hubs may be three seasons.
164.3: Seven ride on a seven-wheeled chariot pulled by seven horses, and seven sisters sing together. The number seven keeps appearing — perhaps the seven priests, seven musical notes or seven rays of the Sun.
164.4: Who saw the first-born when it came into being? How does the 'boneless' (spirit) hold up the 'bony' (the body)? Where is the life and breath of the earth? Who can we ask? Big questions about life itself!
164.5: The poet humbly says, 'I am not wise, so I ask about the hidden places of the gods.' The wise ones have woven seven threads over the young Calf, like weaving a cloth.
164.6: 'Not knowing, I ask those who know — like a student asking a teacher: what is that ONE, unborn, which holds up the six regions of the world?' Asking questions is the first step to wisdom.
164.7: 'Let the one who knows tell us about the home of this lovely Bird.' The Bird may be the Sun. The 'cows' (rays or rain clouds) draw milk from his head and drink water with their feet — like rain falling and being drawn back up.
164.8: The Mother (Earth) and the Father (Sky) come together in thought; she becomes full of life-giving dew, and people come to praise her. The marriage of earth and sky gives life to everything.
164.9: The Mother is yoked to the chariot pole; the Child (perhaps fire or lightning) rests in the wet rows of clouds. The Calf calls to the Mother Cow, who takes all forms in three directions.
164.10: One stands tall carrying three Mothers and three Fathers without tiring — perhaps the three worlds above and below. On the top of the sky they talk in a speech that knows everything.
164.11: A wheel with twelve spokes rolls around the sky and never wears out — the wheel of Ṛta, the true order. Twelve spokes = twelve months. 720 sons in pairs = 360 days and 360 nights!
164.12: Some call him the five-footed Father with twelve forms (the year with five seasons and twelve months), full of water; others say he rides a seven-wheeled, six-spoked chariot (seven days or rays, six seasons).
164.13: On this ever-turning five-spoked wheel all creatures rest. Its axle carries a heavy load but never gets hot, and its hub has never broken since ancient times. Time keeps turning, steady and endless.
164.14: The wheel turns without wearing out; ten pull it on its long pole. The Sun's eye travels through the sky, and all living beings depend on him.
164.15: Among those born together, the seventh is called 'born alone'; the other six are twins, called rishis born of the gods. One explanation: the six seasons in pairs of months, and an extra thirteenth month.
164.16: 'They told me these were males, but they are really females. Whoever has eyes sees it; the blind do not.' The wise son understands it. Riddles teach us that things are not always what they first seem.
164.17: Between the world above and the world below, the Cow has risen with her calf. Where has she gone? Where does she give birth? Perhaps the Cow is Dawn or speech, and the calf is the Sun or a new thought.
164.18: Who knows the father of this Calf, between the upper and lower worlds? Who can say where the divine mind came from? The poet keeps asking about the source of things.
164.19: Those coming towards us are called 'going away', and those going away are called 'coming' — perhaps the planets or seasons that seem to move both ways. Indra and Soma made them move like horses yoked to the sky.
164.20: The most famous image: TWO BIRDS, close friends, sit on the same tree. One eats the sweet fruit; the other just watches without eating. Later the Upaniṣads explained this as two parts of us — one that acts and enjoys, and one that quietly watches.
164.21: Where those birds sing forever of their share of immortality, there is the great Guardian of the universe — and that wise one has come into me, a simple person. Wisdom can live inside anyone.
164.22: On the tree where the birds eat sweetness and raise their young, the sweetest fruit is at the top — but nobody reaches it without knowing the Father. The highest sweetness comes from deep understanding.
164.23: This verse is about the meters: Gāyatrī built on Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh from Triṣṭubh, Jagatī on Jagatī. Those who know how the poems are built are said to gain immortality. The rishis thought rhythm was sacred.
164.24: With the Gāyatrī he measures the hymn, with the hymn the song, with the Triṣṭubh the triplet; with syllables they make seven meters. The Vedas were built carefully, like music.
164.25: With the Jagatī he fixed the flood in the sky, and he saw the Sun in the Rathantara song. The Gāyatrī has three sticks for kindling — three lines — so it is especially strong.
164.26: 'I call the milk cow, so the skilful milker can milk her. May Savitṛ inspire us. The pot is heated; I will speak!' The cow here may also stand for inspired speech that 'gives' poems.
164.27: The cow, lady of treasures, comes lowing and longing for her calf. May she give milk for the twin Aśvins and help us greatly.
164.28: A tender picture: the mother cow moos for her little blinking calf, licks his forehead and calls him to drink her warm milk. The rishis loved watching animals and their care for their young.
164.29: Something hums around the cow as she lows towards the rain-giver; with her cries she humbles people and, turning into lightning, throws off her covering. Perhaps a picture of the storm cloud and lightning.
164.30: That which has breath and life rests firmly in the middle of homes. The Immortal One (perhaps the soul, or fire) is the brother of the mortal body. Something in us never dies.
164.31: 'I saw the Herdsman who never stumbles, coming and going on his paths' — the Sun, travelling through the worlds day after day, dressed in light.
164.32: The one who made him does not fully understand him; he is hidden from the one who saw him. Wrapped inside his Mother, the source of much life, he disappears. Another mystery about birth and creation.
164.33: 'The Sky is my Father; this great Earth is my Mother and my family.' Between the two halves of the world is our birthplace. A lovely reminder that we belong to nature.
164.34: The poet asks: 'Where is the farthest end of the earth? Where is the centre of the world?' (Griffith's translation shortens this verse.)
164.35: The answer: 'This altar is the end of the earth; this worship of ours is the centre of the world.' Wherever we stand doing something sacred is the centre. Soma is the life-seed, and prayer is the highest heaven where Speech lives.
164.36: Seven unripe seeds of the sky keep the world going by Viṣṇu's rule. Full of wisdom and thought, they surround us on every side.
164.37: An honest line: 'I don't clearly know what I really am. I wander around, puzzled in my mind.' Only when the first-born of truth came to him did he get a share of this speech. Even great seers felt unsure!
164.38: The Immortal and the mortal are brothers; they move back and forth, always in opposite directions. People notice one (the body) but not the other (the spirit).
164.39: The gods rest on the syllable of the hymn as on their highest heaven. Someone who doesn't understand it — what use is the hymn to him? But those who understand sit here together. Knowing the meaning matters, not just the sound.
164.40: A gentle blessing for a cow: 'May you be happy with good grass and may we be rich too. Eat grass in every season and come to drink clear water.'
164.41: The buffalo-cow (Speech) lows, making waters flow — with one foot, two, four, eight, nine — and has a thousand syllables in the highest heaven. Speech grows from simple to rich and wonderful.
164.42: From her flow the seas; from her the four directions get their life. From her flows the never-ending stream, and the whole universe lives. Words and knowledge are like a river that feeds the world.
164.43: 'Far away I saw smoke rising from the fire.' People prepared the offering as was the custom in olden times. The poet remembers the old ways of worship.
164.44: Three with long hair appear in their seasons; one shaves at the end of the year, one watches over the world, and one is felt like a breeze but not seen. Perhaps Agni (fire), the Sun and Vāyu (wind).
164.45: Speech has four parts. The wise know them all; three parts stay hidden deep inside, and people speak only the fourth. There is much more to language and thought than what we say aloud.
164.46: THE MOST FAMOUS LINE: 'They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and the heavenly bird Garutmān. Truth is One — the wise call it by many names.' (ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti). Different names, one reality.
164.47: The path down is dark; golden birds fly up to the sky wrapped in water and come down again from the seat of order, soaking the earth. A beautiful riddle about the water cycle: evaporation, clouds and rain!
164.48: Twelve rims, one wheel, three hubs — who understands it? In it are fixed 360 spokes that never come loose. The year: twelve months, three seasons and 360 days!
164.49: 'O Sarasvatī, bring your never-empty breast of joy, with which you feed all good things — giver of wealth and treasure — so we may drink.' Sarasvatī is a river and the goddess of knowledge.
164.50: The gods worshipped through worship itself; these were the first rules. The great ones reached the highest heaven where the old gods, the Sādhyas, live. (This verse also appears in the Puruṣa Sukta.)
164.51: The same water rises and falls again day after day. The rain-clouds give life to the earth, and the fires bring life to the sky. Nature keeps everything moving in a circle.
164.52: 'I call Sarasvān, the great heavenly Bird with beautiful wings, the seed of plants and waters, who makes us happy with rain at the right time, to help us.' The riddle hymn ends with a prayer for timely rain.
